The book of ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ opens with a defeat. In the third year of ⟦p:jehoiakim_1085|Jehoiakim⟧, king of Judah, ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ comes to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and some of the sacred vessels of the temple are carried off to the treasury of a Babylonian god. With them go a number of young men from Judah's royal family and nobility, taken to be trained for service in the court of their conqueror. One of them is Daniel.

The year is about six hundred and five before Christ. ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧, the crown prince of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, had just defeated the Egyptian army at Carchemish on the ⟦l:euphrates_421|Euphrates⟧, and within months he would be king. Babylon was now the great power of the Near East, heir to the Assyrian empire it had helped to destroy. This first deportation from Judah was small, a matter of hostages and promising youths. A larger one would follow eight years later, when the prophet ⟦p:ezekiel_1237|Ezekiel⟧ was taken, and in five hundred and eighty-six the city and temple would be destroyed. ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧, then, belongs to the same generation as Ezekiel, and Ezekiel mentions him by name. But where Ezekiel lived among the exiles by a canal in the countryside, Daniel lived in the capital itself, at the centre of imperial power.

The book follows him for about seventy years, through the reigns of several kings. ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧, the most powerful ruler of his age, dominates the early chapters. Then comes ⟦p:belshazzar_437|Belshazzar⟧, who rules in ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ while his father Nabonidus is away, and who is the last to reign there. Then, after Babylon falls to the ⟦l:media_776|Medes⟧ and Persians in five hundred and thirty-nine, the scene shifts to the new Persian empire, with ⟦p:darius_980|Darius the Mede⟧, and ⟦p:cyrus_968|Cyrus⟧, the Persian king who allowed the exiles to return home. ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ is last seen in the third year of Cyrus, an old man still in Babylon.

The book falls into two halves. The first six chapters are stories, told about ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ and his three friends, ⟦p:shadrach_1398|Hananiah⟧, ⟦p:meshach_2092|Mishael⟧ and ⟦p:azariah_545|Azariah⟧, better known by their Babylonian names ⟦p:shadrach_1398|Shadrach⟧, ⟦p:meshach_2092|Meshach⟧ and ⟦p:azariah_545|Abednego⟧. They are stories of the court: a test of diet, a king's dream that no one else can interpret, a golden statue and a blazing furnace, a king driven mad, a feast interrupted by writing on the wall, and a den of lions. In each, faithful Jews living in a foreign land face pressure to compromise, and in each the God of Israel shows himself greater than the kings of the earth.

The last six chapters are visions, told by ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ himself. He sees four great beasts rising from the sea, a ram and a goat, a heavenly messenger who explains the seventy weeks, and finally a long revelation of wars between kings of the north and the south. These visions survey the empires that will follow ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, and they look ahead to a time of great suffering for God's people and to the final establishment of God's own kingdom. Some of the kingdoms are named in the text itself: Babylon, ⟦l:media_776|Media⟧ and ⟦l:persia_938|Persia⟧, and ⟦l:greece_495|Greece⟧. The visions are dated within Daniel's own lifetime, and they are not all in order with the stories. The first two visions come from the reign of ⟦p:belshazzar_437|Belshazzar⟧, before the events of chapter five.

The book has another curious feature. It is written in two languages. It begins in Hebrew, switches to Aramaic, the international language of the empire, in the middle of chapter two, and returns to Hebrew at chapter eight. The Aramaic section covers the chapters most concerned with the nations and their kings.

The book comes from ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ himself, in the sixth century before Christ, and its later visions look far ahead, describing in detail the reign of the Greek king Antiochus the Fourth, who persecuted the Jews in the second century. Through it all runs one message: the kingdoms of this world rise and fall, but the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind.

In the Hebrew Bible, ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ is placed among the Writings rather than the Prophets. In Christian Bibles it follows ⟦p:ezekiel_1237|Ezekiel⟧ as the last of the major prophets. Its influence reaches far into the New Testament. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ speaks of the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, and his favourite way of referring to himself, the Son of Man, comes from Daniel's seventh chapter. The book of Revelation draws on Daniel's visions throughout.
1:
⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ and the other young captives have arrived in ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, and the opening chapter shows what their new life will demand. The young men from Judah are placed under Ashpenaz, the chief of the court officials, and given a three-year course in the language and literature of the Chaldeans, the learned class of Babylon, whose studies included astronomy, omens and divination. They are to eat from the king's own table, and then serve in the palace.

Four are named: ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧, ⟦p:shadrach_1398|Hananiah⟧, ⟦p:meshach_2092|Mishael⟧ and ⟦p:azariah_545|Azariah⟧. Each Hebrew name contains a reference to the God of Israel, and each is replaced with a Babylonian one. Daniel becomes ⟦p:daniel_975|Belteshazzar⟧, a name that calls on the protection of a Babylonian god, and his friends become ⟦p:shadrach_1398|Shadrach⟧, ⟦p:meshach_2092|Meshach⟧ and ⟦p:azariah_545|Abednego⟧.

⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ accepts the new name and the new education, but he draws a line at the king's food and wine. He resolves not to defile himself with it. What follows is a quiet test, lasting ten days. The chapter closes by noting that Daniel remained in royal service until the first year of King ⟦p:cyrus_968|Cyrus⟧, more than sixty years later.
2:
⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ is now king, in the second year of his reign, and he is troubled by dreams. Dreams were taken seriously as messages from the gods, and ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ had a whole class of experts to interpret them. The king summons them, but he sets an impossible condition. They must tell him not only what the dream means, but what the dream was.

When the astrologers reply, the book itself changes language. From the middle of this chapter to the end of chapter seven, ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ is written in Aramaic, the common language of the Near East.

The experts protest that no one but the gods could do what the king asks, and the furious king orders all the wise men of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ to be executed, including ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ and his friends. Daniel asks for time, and the four pray together for mercy from the God of heaven. That night the mystery is revealed. The dream concerns a great statue made of different metals, and a stone cut out without human hands, and it looks far beyond ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧'s own reign to what will happen in the latter days.
3:
⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ has acknowledged ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧'s God as the God of gods, and Daniel's three friends have been made administrators in the province of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. This chapter carries no date, and Daniel himself does not appear in it. It belongs to his three friends, known here only by their Babylonian names.

The king sets up a golden statue, sixty cubits high and six wide, about ninety feet tall, on the plain of ⟦l:dura_347|Dura⟧ in the province of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. The text does not say whom it represented. Every official in the empire is summoned to its dedication, and the lists of officials and instruments, repeated again and again, give the scene the ponderous grandeur of a state occasion. When the music sounds, everyone must fall down and worship. The penalty for refusal is the blazing furnace.

Some of the astrologers see their opportunity and report that certain Jews have refused. ⟦p:shadrach_1398|Shadrach⟧, ⟦p:meshach_2092|Meshach⟧ and ⟦p:azariah_545|Abednego⟧ are brought before the furious king, and their reply is one of the most famous answers in the Bible. Their God is able to deliver them, they say, but even if he does not, they will not serve the king's gods.
4:
This chapter is unusual in the Bible. It is written as a royal proclamation, issued by ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ himself to all the peoples of the earth, and most of it is told in his own words. He begins by praising the Most High God, and then explains why.

He was at ease in his palace, at the height of his power, when another dream alarmed him. Only ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ could interpret it. ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ describes a great tree reaching to the sky, sheltering every creature, and a holy messenger from heaven, a watcher, who orders it to be cut down, leaving only a stump bound with iron and bronze. The one represented by the tree will live like an animal until seven periods of time pass over him.

⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ is troubled by what it means, and with good reason, because the tree is the king. He urges ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧ to turn from his sins and show mercy to the oppressed. A year later, walking on the roof of his palace, the king looks out over ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ and boasts of the great city he has built by his own power. He had indeed rebuilt Babylon on a magnificent scale. While the words are still in his mouth, a voice speaks from heaven.
5:
Some time has passed since the stories of ⟦p:nebuchadnezzar_2167|Nebuchadnezzar⟧. He died in five hundred and sixty-two before Christ, and after several short reigns the throne passed to Nabonidus, a king who spent years away from his capital, leaving his son ⟦p:belshazzar_437|Belshazzar⟧ to rule in ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. Belshazzar is called here the son of Nebuchadnezzar, a title that in the language of the time was used of a successor or descendant. ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧, now in his eighties, is no longer at the king's side, and he will have to be sent for.

The scene is a great banquet for a thousand nobles. In the background, though the chapter does not pause to say so, the armies of ⟦p:cyrus_968|Cyrus⟧ the Persian are closing in on ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. ⟦p:belshazzar_437|Belshazzar⟧, drinking, orders the gold and silver vessels from the temple in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ to be brought in, the vessels of the book's opening verses, and the guests drink from them as they praise their gods.

Then the fingers of a human hand appear and write on the plastered wall of the palace. None of the king's wise men can read it. Then the queen comes into the hall, and she remembers ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧. The king offers him the reward of third ruler in the kingdom, because Nabonidus and ⟦p:belshazzar_437|Belshazzar⟧ held the first two places. What happens next is over before the night is out.
6:
⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ has fallen, and a new empire rules. The kingdom has passed to ⟦p:darius_980|Darius the Mede⟧. The new administration has a hundred and twenty satraps, or provincial governors, with three senior administrators over them. ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧, now very old, is one of the three, and the king plans to set him over the whole kingdom.

His rivals look for something to accuse him of and find nothing. So they turn to his faith. They persuade the king to sign a decree that for thirty days no one may pray to any god or man except the king, and, in accordance with the law of the ⟦l:media_776|Medes⟧ and Persians, it cannot be changed. The penalty is the den of lions.

⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ learns of the decree and goes home. In his upper room the windows open towards ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, as ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧ had once asked that the exiles might pray towards the city, and three times a day he kneels and prays, as he always has. The king soon finds he has been trapped by his own law.
7:
Here the stories of the court give way to visions, and the book steps back in time. The first vision comes in the first year of ⟦p:belshazzar_437|Belshazzar⟧, before the feast of chapter five, while ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ still ruled. ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ now speaks in his own voice.

The four winds of heaven stir up the great sea, and four beasts rise from it, each unlike the others: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear, a leopard with four wings and four heads, and a fourth beast, terrifying and unlike any animal, with iron teeth and ten horns. Among its horns a little horn appears, with eyes and a boastful mouth.

Then the scene moves to heaven. Thrones are set in place, the Ancient of Days takes his seat, and the books are opened. And one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given an everlasting kingdom. The beasts, ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ is told, are four kings and their kingdoms, the same succession of empires that the statue of chapter two set out in gold, silver, bronze and iron. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ would take up the figure of the son of man coming with the clouds when he stood on trial before the high priest.
8:
Two years after the vision of the four beasts, in the third year of ⟦p:belshazzar_437|Belshazzar⟧, ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ has a second vision. At this point the book returns from Aramaic to Hebrew, and it stays in Hebrew to the end.

In the vision ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ finds himself at ⟦l:susa_1118|Susa⟧, by the Ulai canal, in the land of ⟦l:elam_365|Elam⟧, east of ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧. Susa would later become a royal capital of the Persian empire, the setting of the book of ⟦p:esther_1343|Esther⟧ and of Nehemiah's service at court.

He sees a ram with two horns, one longer than the other, charging west, north and south. Then a goat with a single great horn comes from the west, so fast it does not touch the ground, and shatters the ram. This time the angel ⟦p:gabriel_1261|Gabriel⟧, named here for the first time in the Bible, explains the vision, and names the kingdoms. The ram is the kings of ⟦l:media_776|Media⟧ and ⟦l:persia_938|Persia⟧, the goat is ⟦l:greece_495|Greece⟧, and its great horn is the first king, Alexander the Great, whose empire split into four after his early death. From one of the four comes a small horn that grows great and attacks the sanctuary. This is Antiochus the Fourth, the Greek king who profaned the temple in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ in the second century before Christ.
9:
The scene moves forward again, to the first year of ⟦p:darius_980|Darius the Mede⟧, the year ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ fell to the Persians, around five hundred and thirty-nine before Christ. The den of lions belongs to this same period, and so does the decree of ⟦p:cyrus_968|Cyrus⟧, recorded in ⟦p:ezra_1245|Ezra⟧, allowing the exiles to go home.

⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ has been reading the scrolls of the prophet ⟦p:jeremiah_853|Jeremiah⟧, who had written that the desolation of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ would last seventy years. Daniel was taken to ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧ some sixty-six years earlier. The seventy years are nearly over. So he turns to God in prayer, with fasting, sackcloth and ashes, and the prayer that follows takes up most of the chapter. It is a confession for the whole nation, acknowledging that the exile came because Israel would not listen to the prophets, and it appeals only to God's mercy and the honour of his name.

While he is still praying, at the hour of the evening sacrifice, though no sacrifice has been offered in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ for decades, ⟦p:gabriel_1261|Gabriel⟧ comes to him again. He brings a message about seventy weeks, or seventy sevens, decreed for ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧'s people and the holy city, reaching on to the coming of the Messiah, the Prince, who will be cut off, and to a time of desolation.
10:
The final vision of the book fills the last three chapters, and this one sets the scene for it. It is the third year of ⟦p:cyrus_968|Cyrus⟧, king of ⟦l:persia_938|Persia⟧, around five hundred and thirty-six before Christ. By now the first exiles have gone home to Judah, as the book of ⟦p:ezra_1245|Ezra⟧ tells, and have begun to rebuild. ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧, an old man, has stayed behind. This is the last date in his life that the book records.

After three weeks of mourning and fasting, standing on the bank of the great river ⟦l:tigris_1163|Tigris⟧ with some companions, he sees a man dressed in linen, his face like lightning and his voice like the roar of a crowd. The others do not see him, but terror falls on them and they run away. ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ is left alone, and his strength drains from him.

The figure touches him and tells him that his prayer was heard from the first day, but that he was delayed for twenty-one days by the prince of the kingdom of ⟦l:persia_938|Persia⟧, until ⟦p:michael_2068|Michael⟧, one of the chief princes, came to help. It is a rare glimpse of conflict in the unseen world behind the kingdoms of the earth. The messenger has come to tell ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ what will happen to his people in the latter days.
11:
The heavenly messenger now delivers his message, one of the most detailed passages of prediction in the Bible. It names none of the kings it describes, yet it traces their wars and marriages, their alliances and betrayals, so closely that the history of the centuries after ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ can be followed step by step.

It begins with the kings of ⟦l:persia_938|Persia⟧, and then a mighty king rises, only to see his kingdom broken up towards the four winds. From the pieces, two rivals step forward, the king of the South and the king of the North, and the struggle between them runs on through generations. In the history of the following centuries these were the Ptolemies, the Greek dynasty that ruled ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, and the Seleucids, who ruled from ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧. The ⟦l:judah_1280|land of Judah⟧, which the text calls the Beautiful Land, lay between them and was repeatedly fought over.

Then a despicable person seizes the throne of the North by intrigue. This is Antiochus the Fourth, already glimpsed as the small horn of chapter eight, who turns against the holy covenant, desecrates the temple, abolishes the daily sacrifice and sets up the abomination of desolation, while those who know their God stand firm. In the closing verses the vision reaches on to the time of the end.
12:
The last vision of the book reaches its conclusion. After the rise and fall of kings, the messenger turns to what lies at the end of it all.

⟦p:michael_2068|Michael⟧, the great prince who watches over ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧'s people, will arise. There will be a time of distress unlike any before it, but those whose names are written in the book will be delivered. And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. It is the clearest statement of a resurrection of the dead anywhere in the Old Testament.

⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧ is told to seal up the book until the time of the end. Then, standing by the river, he hears one heavenly figure ask the man in linen how long it will be until these things are fulfilled. The answer is a time, times and half a time, followed by numbers of days, and Daniel admits that he does not understand. The book's final words are addressed to him personally. He is to go his way, to rest, and to rise to receive his inheritance at the end of the days.
